title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
summary: What happens during solar and lunar eclipses, why they do not happen every month, and how to watch them safely.
poll: An eclipse is worth staying up late or travelling far to see.

versions.title: When the Sun Goes Dark
versions.text:
The Earth goes around the Sun. The Moon goes around the Earth. We say they orbit.

Now and then, the three line up. Then we get an eclipse.

Look up in the day. The Moon can move in front of the Sun. It can block the Sun. The sky gets dark! The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. This is a solar eclipse.

Do not look at the Sun! It can hurt your eyes. Wear eclipse glasses. They are made for this job.

Now look at the Moon at night. The Earth can get in the way. Its shadow falls on the Moon. This is a lunar eclipse. The Moon may turn red. You can look at it. It is safe.

Why not see one each month? The Moon's path is a bit tilted. So the three do not line up a lot.

A big solar eclipse comes in 2027. It will pass over parts of Saudi Arabia. Get your glasses!

versions.title: When the Sun Goes Dark
versions.text:
The Earth moves around the Sun. The Moon moves around the Earth. We say they orbit.

Now and then, the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon line up. Then we get an eclipse. There are two kinds.

In the day, the Moon can pass in front of the Sun. The Moon can block the Sun's light. The sky gets dark! The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. This is a solar eclipse.

Never look right at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes. Wear special eclipse glasses. They keep your eyes safe.

At night, the Earth can get between the Sun and the Moon. Then the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. This is a lunar eclipse. The Moon may turn a dark red. It is safe to look at with just your eyes.

Why is there not an eclipse each month? The Moon's path is a bit tilted. So the three do not line up very often.

In 2027, a big solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia. Many people will watch it with their glasses on.

versions.title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun. At the same time, the Moon travels around the Earth. We say they orbit.

Now and then, the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon line up in a row. Then an eclipse happens. There are two kinds of eclipse.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes in front of the Sun. The Moon blocks the Sun's light, and its shadow falls on the Earth. The sky can get as dark as night for a few minutes!

You must never look right at the Sun, because it can hurt your eyes. Wear special eclipse glasses. Normal sunglasses are not safe.

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon often turns a dark red color. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with just your eyes.

Why is there not an eclipse every month? The Moon's path is a little tilted. So the three only line up once in a while.

In 2027, a big solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia. Many families will watch it with their eclipse glasses on.

versions.title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun once a year. At the same time, the Moon travels around the Earth about once a month. We say the Moon and the Earth orbit.

Once in a while, the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon line up in a straight row. When this happens, we see an eclipse. There are two main kinds.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. The Moon blocks the Sun's light, and its shadow falls on part of the Earth. If the Sun is fully covered, the sky turns dark for a few minutes, and birds may go quiet.

Never look straight at the Sun, because it can badly hurt your eyes. Wear special eclipse glasses. Normal sunglasses are not safe enough.

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow slowly covers the Moon, which often turns a dark red color. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with just your eyes.

Why is there not an eclipse every month? The Moon's path around the Earth is a little tilted. So most months, the three do not line up.

In 2027, a large solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia. Many families will watch it with eclipse glasses on.

versions.title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun once a year, and the Moon travels around the Earth about once a month. Usually, these three bodies are not in a straight line. But once in a while, they align, and we see an eclipse.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. The Moon blocks the Sun's light, and its shadow falls on part of the Earth. If the Moon covers only part of the Sun, it is a partial eclipse. If it covers the whole Sun, it is a total eclipse. During a total eclipse, the sky turns dark for a few minutes. People can then see the corona, the Sun's thin outer layer, glowing around the black Moon.

You must never look straight at the Sun, because it can badly hurt your eyes. Wear certified eclipse glasses. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe enough.

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow slowly covers the Moon. The Moon often turns a dark red color. This happens because Earth's atmosphere bends some red sunlight into the shadow. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with just your eyes. Anyone on the night side of the Earth can see it.

A total solar eclipse is different. The Moon's dark shadow is small, so it only covers a narrow strip of the Earth.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's path is a little tilted. Today, scientists can predict eclipses many years ahead. For example, they know that a total solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia in August 2027.

versions.title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun once a year, while the Moon circles the Earth about once a month. Usually, these three bodies are not arranged in a straight line. Occasionally, however, they align, and an eclipse takes place.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. The Moon blocks the sunlight, and its shadow falls on part of the Earth's surface. If the Moon covers only part of the Sun, the eclipse is partial. If it covers the entire Sun, the eclipse is total. During a total eclipse, the daytime sky darkens for a few minutes, and observers can see the corona, the Sun's delicate outer layer, glowing around the black Moon.

Never look directly at the Sun, because it can permanently damage your eyes. Always wear certified eclipse glasses, since ordinary sunglasses are not nearly protective enough.

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow gradually covers the Moon. The Moon frequently turns a coppery red color, because Earth's atmosphere bends some red sunlight into the shadow. A lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with your eyes, and anyone on the night side of the Earth can observe it.

A total solar eclipse is different. The Moon's darkest shadow is relatively small, so it covers only a narrow strip of the Earth's surface.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted. Today, astronomers can predict eclipses many years in advance. They already know that a total solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia in August 2027.

versions.title: Eclipses of the Sun and Moon
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun once a year, while the Moon circles the Earth approximately once a month. Usually, these three bodies are not arranged in a straight line, but occasionally they align, and an eclipse takes place.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the sunlight and casting its shadow on part of the Earth's surface. If the Moon covers only part of the Sun, the eclipse is partial. If it covers the entire Sun, the eclipse is total. During a total eclipse, the daytime sky darkens for a few minutes, and observers can see the corona, the Sun's delicate outer layer, glowing around the black disk of the Moon.

Never look directly at the Sun, because its intense light can permanently damage your eyes. Always wear certified eclipse glasses, since ordinary sunglasses are not nearly protective enough.

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow gradually covers the Moon. The Moon frequently turns a coppery red color, because Earth's atmosphere bends some red sunlight into the shadow. A lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with your eyes, and anyone on the night side of the planet can observe it.

A total solar eclipse is different, because the Moon's darkest shadow is relatively small and covers only a narrow strip of the Earth's surface.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted compared with the Earth's. Today, astronomers can predict eclipses with remarkable accuracy many years in advance. They already know, for instance, that a total solar eclipse will cross parts of Saudi Arabia in August 2027.

versions.title: Eclipses: When Shadows Cross the Sky
versions.text:
The Earth travels around the Sun once a year, while the Moon circles the Earth roughly once a month. Usually, these three bodies are not arranged in a straight line, but occasionally they line up exactly, and an eclipse takes place.

A solar eclipse happens at new moon, when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and casts its shadow on part of the Earth's surface. Total solar eclipses are possible because of a remarkable coincidence. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times farther away, so both look almost the same size in our sky. During totality, the brief period when the Sun is completely hidden, the daytime sky darkens and the glowing corona appears around the black Moon.

Sometimes the Moon is near the farthest point of its orbit and looks slightly smaller than the Sun. Then it cannot cover the Sun completely, and a bright ring of sunlight remains. This is called an annular eclipse.

Never look directly at the Sun, because its light can permanently damage your eyes, so always wear certified eclipse glasses.

A lunar eclipse happens at full moon, when the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. During totality, the Moon often turns coppery red, because Earth's atmosphere can refract, or bend, red sunlight into the shadow. Anyone on the night side of the planet can safely watch it.

Long ago, eclipses frightened many people, who could not explain why the Sun suddenly disappeared. Over the centuries, careful observers, including astronomers of the Islamic world, recorded eclipses in detail and improved mathematical methods for calculating the movements of the Sun and Moon. Modern scientists still travel to total eclipses, because the corona is normally invisible in the overwhelming glare of the Sun.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees compared with Earth's orbit. Because the Moon's shadow covers only a narrow path, astronomers can predict exactly where totality will be seen, such as parts of Saudi Arabia in August 2027.

versions.title: Eclipses: When Shadows Cross the Sky
versions.text:
The Earth revolves around the Sun once a year, while the Moon circles the Earth approximately once a month. Ordinarily, these three bodies are not arranged in a straight line, but occasionally they align precisely, and an eclipse takes place.

A solar eclipse occurs at new moon, when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and casts its shadow on a portion of the Earth's surface. Total solar eclipses are possible because of an extraordinary coincidence: the Sun is approximately 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also approximately 400 times farther away, so both appear almost identical in size in our sky. During totality, the brief interval when the Sun is completely concealed, the daytime sky darkens dramatically, and the shimmering corona becomes visible surrounding the black lunar disk.

Occasionally the Moon is near the most distant point of its orbit and appears slightly smaller than the Sun. Consequently, it cannot conceal the Sun entirely, leaving a brilliant ring of sunlight, a phenomenon known as an annular eclipse.

Never look directly at the Sun, because its intense radiation can permanently damage your eyes, so always wear certified eclipse glasses.

A lunar eclipse occurs at full moon, when the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. During totality, the Moon frequently turns coppery red, because Earth's atmosphere can refract, or bend, reddish sunlight into the shadow. Anyone on the night side of the planet can safely observe it without protection.

Historically, eclipses terrified many communities, who could not explain why the Sun suddenly vanished. Over the centuries, meticulous observers, including astronomers of the Islamic world, documented eclipses carefully and refined mathematical techniques for calculating the movements of the Sun and Moon. Contemporary scientists still travel enormous distances to witness total eclipses, because the corona is ordinarily invisible in the overwhelming glare of the solar surface.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's orbit is tilted approximately five degrees relative to Earth's orbit. Since the Moon's shadow covers only a narrow path, astronomers can calculate precisely where totality will be visible, including portions of Saudi Arabia in August 2027, an event that will probably attract enthusiastic observers from many countries.

versions.title: Eclipses: When Shadows Cross the Sky
versions.text:
The Earth revolves around the Sun once a year, while the Moon circles the Earth approximately once a month. Ordinarily, these three celestial bodies are not arranged in a straight line, but occasionally they align precisely, and an eclipse takes place.

A solar eclipse occurs at new moon, when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and casts its shadow on a portion of the Earth's surface. Total solar eclipses are possible because of an extraordinary coincidence: the Sun is approximately 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also approximately 400 times farther away, so both appear almost identical in size in our sky. During totality, the brief interval when the Sun is completely concealed, the daytime sky darkens dramatically, temperatures drop noticeably, and the shimmering corona becomes visible surrounding the black lunar disk.

Occasionally the Moon is near the most distant point of its elliptical orbit and therefore appears slightly smaller than the Sun. Consequently, it cannot conceal the Sun entirely, leaving a brilliant ring of sunlight, a phenomenon known as an annular eclipse.

Never look directly at the Sun, because its intense radiation can permanently damage your eyes, so always wear certified eclipse glasses or use an indirect viewing method such as a pinhole projector.

A lunar eclipse occurs at full moon, when the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon. During totality, the Moon frequently turns coppery red, because Earth's atmosphere can refract, or bend, reddish sunlight into the shadow, producing the same colors we associate with sunrise and sunset. Anyone on the night side of the planet can safely observe it without protection.

Historically, eclipses terrified numerous communities, who could not explain why the Sun suddenly vanished. Over the centuries, meticulous observers, including astronomers of the Islamic world, documented eclipses systematically and refined mathematical techniques for calculating the movements of the Sun and Moon. Contemporary scientists still travel enormous distances to witness total eclipses, because the corona is ordinarily invisible in the overwhelming glare of the solar surface, and studying it reveals information about the Sun's magnetic activity.

Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's orbit is tilted approximately five degrees relative to Earth's orbit. Since the Moon's shadow covers only a narrow path, astronomers can calculate precisely where totality will be visible, including portions of Saudi Arabia in August 2027, an event that will probably attract enthusiastic observers from numerous countries.
